extracted.intended_audience: school and college administrators, Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel, and other recipients of Federal education funds
extracted.subtask_short: defining sexual harassment under Title IX
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory interpretation of §106.30 (Title IX) defining sexual harassment for recipients of Federal education funds, explaining applicable elements (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive, denial of equal access), per-se categories, and interaction with free speech and institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.30 definition of sexual harassment (revised wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment includes “unwelcome conduct” on the basis of sex “determined by a reasonable person” to be so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal educational access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Department's revised formulation of the Davis standard incorporated into §106.30. It captures both single severe incidents (where applicable) and courses of conduct that meet the elements; the definition is meant to set a threshold over which unwelcome conduct becomes actionable under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective unwelcomeness vs. objective elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Davis standard as formulated in §106.30 is subjective with respect to the unwelcomeness of the conduct (i.e., whether the complainant viewed the conduct as unwelcome), but elements of severity, pervasiveness, objective offensiveness, and denial of equal access are determined by a reasonable person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must accept a complainant's report that conduct was unwelcome, but then assess whether the conduct meets the other elements from the vantage of a reasonable person in the complainant's shoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per se actionable categories (quid pro quo and Clery Act/VAWA offenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo harassment and Clery Act/VAWA offenses (sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking) constitute sexual harassment under §106.30 without any evaluation for pervasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are treated as per se sex discrimination/actionable harassment to ensure recipients address serious problems promptly; they do not need to meet the severe/pervasive/objectively offensive threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable person standard for severity/pervasiveness/objective offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether conduct is severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive (and whether it results in denial of equal access) is determined under a reasonable person standard, i.e., by a reasonable person standing in the shoes of the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reasonable person analysis allows consideration of circumstances facing the particular complainant (age, disability status, sex, and other characteristics) but the Department declined to require separate male/female-perspective tests or to invite sex stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient flexibility to define consent and related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain flexibility to define consent and terms commonly used to describe absence or negation of consent (e.g., incapacity, coercion, threat of force), recognizing state-law requirements and community values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to list verbal sexual coercion as an element of sexual harassment/assault in §106.30, leaving recipients discretion to incorporate such definitions in their local policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional speech and publication of internal examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from publishing a list of situations the recipient has found to meet §106.30, advising potential victims/perpetrators that particular conduct violates Title IX, or creating a list of situations violating the recipient's own code of conduct even if not Title IX violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may use institutional speech to educate the community about prohibited conduct and expectations without conflicting with the regulatory definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible institutional responses when allegations do not meet §106.30
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory dismissal of a formal complaint because the allegations do not constitute sexual harassment under §106.30 does not preclude a recipient from acting on the allegations through the recipient's code of conduct; recipients may also provide supportive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(3) clarifies that dismissal for not meeting Title IX's definition still permits non-Title IX discipline, supportive measures, institutional speech, and programming to address the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures may be provided regardless of Title IX applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations permit a recipient to provide supportive measures to a complainant even where the conduct alleged does not meet the §106.30 definition of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to offer accommodations, assistance, or other supportive actions even when no Title IX investigation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microaggressions and lower-level offensive conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to prohibit microaggressions per se under Title IX, but notes such acts could form part of a course of conduct that meets the severity/pervasiveness/objective offensiveness standard and that recipients may address microaggressions under non-Title IX conduct codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools may address microaggressions through supportive measures, institutional speech, and programming; Title IX liability attaches only where the Davis elements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold concept for actionable harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 sets a threshold over which a person's unwelcome conduct constitutes sexual harassment; while some harassment does not meet the threshold, serious incidents that jeopardize equal educational access exceed it and are actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The threshold is designed to balance protection from sex discrimination with protection of free speech and academic freedom; recipients may still intervene on non-actionable conduct through other policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific analysis required; examples not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether particular conduct meets the Davis standard cannot be resolved by categorical examples; determinations are fact-specific and require consideration of aggregate impact (not disaggregated allegations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to issue definitive statements about hypothetical examples, noting that circumstances (e.g., dissemination of revenge porn, conspiracies to harass, teacher-student coercion) may or may not meet the standard depending on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of First Amendment chill via application of Davis standard to speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech and expression that are unwelcome must be evaluated for severity, pervasiveness, objective offensiveness, and denial of equal access; applying the Davis standard to speech-based harassment avoids unconstitutionally restricting free speech and academic freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that broadly worded anti-harassment policies risk chilling protected speech; the regulatory approach treats non-speech conduct broadly while requiring the Davis threshold for verbal conduct to balance Title IX and First Amendment concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of 'severe' element considers complainant's circumstances; no burden to 'prove' severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Severity is a necessary element and is evaluated under a reasonable person standard that takes into account circumstances facing the complainant (age, disability, sex, etc.); a complainant need only describe what occurred and the recipient assesses severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejected the notion that survivors must 'prove' severity; the recipient conducts the objective assessment after the complainant describes the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pervasiveness element and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pervasiveness is part of the Davis formulation for many harassment claims, but does not apply to per se categories (quid pro quo and Clery Act/VAWA offenses); pervasive conduct may include widespread dissemination or multiple perpetrators acting in concert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should recognize that single instances of certain physical conduct may be actionable under other laws even if not meeting §106.30 prongs; pervasiveness must be evaluated in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective offensiveness evaluated in aggregate and with reasonable-person viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether conduct is 'objectively offensive' is judged by a reasonable person standing in the shoes of the complainant, considering aggregate/cumulative impact rather than disaggregating allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to define 'objectively offensive' as oxymoronic; evaluation should focus on what a reasonable person in the complainant's position would find offensive, without imposing male/female perspective tests or codifying identity-based stereotypes.
